name: Ipamorelin

lead: Ipamorelin is a synthetic pentapeptide that selectively stimulates growth hormone release. Novo Nordisk developed it in the 1990s, and it is now sold as a research peptide.

Clinical work has been limited, mainly early pharmacology and a trial in post-surgical bowel recovery that showed no clear benefit. Good human data supporting claims for muscle and fat loss have not been published.

paras: It is a selective agonist of the ghrelin receptor (GHS-R1a), triggering pulsatile pituitary growth hormone release with relatively little effect on cortisol and prolactin compared with older secretagogues.

It is not approved for human use and is banned in sport. Short-term data are limited; theoretical concerns include insulin resistance, fluid retention and effects of long-term GH/IGF-1 elevation. Product quality is unregulated.

lead: Ipamorelin (development code NNC 26-0161) is a synthetic pentapeptide that stimulates the release of growth hormone (GH) by acting as a selective agonist at the ghrelin receptor, also called the growth hormone secretagogue receptor. It was derived from the earlier compound GHRP-1 and originally developed by Novo Nordisk in the 1990s.[1][2]

It was described in 1998 as the first selective GH secretagogue because, unlike older peptides such as GHRP-6 and GHRP-2, it raises GH without a notable rise in cortisol or ACTH, and it does not affect prolactin, FSH, LH or TSH.[1][2] Clinical development, led by Helsinn Therapeutics, focused on postoperative ileus (a post-surgical bowel dysfunction) and was discontinued for lack of efficacy.[1][3]

Ipamorelin is not an approved medicine. It is sold as a research peptide, used by some athletes and physique enthusiasts, and prohibited in sport.[1][4] Reviews of peptides used in sport and aesthetic medicine describe human evidence of cosmetic or performance benefit as limited, with most data coming from short-term pharmacology studies and animal work.[5][6][7]

paras: Ipamorelin binds the ghrelin/growth hormone secretagogue receptor (GHS-R1a) in the pituitary and hypothalamus, triggering GH release; Grokipedia describes activation of phospholipase C and calcium signalling downstream of the receptor.[1][8] A 1998 pharmacology report characterised ipamorelin as the first GH secretagogue with high selectivity for GH, comparable to GHRH in lacking cortisol and ACTH release, whereas GHRP-6 and GHRP-2 stimulate those hormones.[1][2] Unlike ghrelin, ipamorelin is reported to have a less pronounced effect on appetite, though this characterisation comes from a secondary source.[8]

A randomized dose-escalation trial in healthy men infused ipamorelin over 15 minutes at five dose levels with eight volunteers per level, and found dose-proportional pharmacokinetics with a short plasma half-life, with GH rising in response.[9] Grokipedia reports a half-life of about two hours after subcutaneous administration.[8]
Human trials of ipamorelin are few and have focused on pharmacology and on a gastrointestinal indication, not on appearance or muscle.
Pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic modelling: The 1999 dose-escalation study in healthy men characterised the peptide's pharmacokinetics and the resulting GH response.[9]

Postoperative ileus: A multicentre, double-blind, randomized, phase II proof-of-concept trial (NCT00672074, 117 participants) tested ipamorelin as a ghrelin-receptor agonist for recovery of gut function after bowel resection.[3][10] A second phase II study (NCT01280344, 320 participants) tested it against placebo for recovery of gastrointestinal function.[11] Wikipedia reports the programme was discontinued because of lack of efficacy.[1]

Animal studies: In rats, ipamorelin induced longitudinal bone growth, and in GH-deficient mice it produced a small increase in body weight and fat pad mass that appeared independent of GH, a finding the authors framed as GH-independent stimulation of adiposity.[12][13][1] In ferrets, ipamorelin and anamorelin inhibited cisplatin-induced weight loss.[14]

No trial has tested ipamorelin for muscle growth, fat loss, skin or other cosmetic outcomes in healthy people. Reviews note that most peptide studies examine therapeutic dosing, and that evidence for the CJC-1295 and ipamorelin combination in sports and orthopaedic contexts is limited.[5][6][15]

Because no long-term human trials exist, safety in healthy people is described as unknown. A review of peptide use in sport and bodybuilding lists potential cardiovascular strain, insulin resistance, dyslipidemia and psychiatric instability for peptide classes including ipamorelin, and warns that products from unregulated supply chains may be mislabeled or contaminated.[5][4] Reviews of GH secretagogues note that data on clinical effects are scarce.[15][7]
Theoretical concerns discussed in the literature relate to sustained GH and IGF-1 elevation, insulin sensitivity and fluid retention, as with GH-axis drugs generally.[15][7]

Ipamorelin was derived from GHRP-1 by researchers at Novo Nordisk, who reported it in 1998 as the first selective GH secretagogue.[1][2] Pharmacokinetic work in volunteers followed in 1999.[9] Helsinn Therapeutics took it into phase II trials for postoperative ileus beginning in 2008, and a second trial started in 2011, but the programme was discontinued.[1][10][11]

Wikipedia records that ipamorelin has been used by athletes as a performance-enhancing drug and is commonly marketed as a research peptide rather than as a pharmaceutical.[1] The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits growth hormone-releasing peptides, and analytical chemistry papers describe methods to detect growth hormone releasing peptides and their metabolites in urine for doping control.[4] A 2026 review notes that peptides including ipamorelin are marketed as more selective and ostensibly safer alternatives to anabolic steroids, while stating that clinical evidence supporting their use in sport is limited.[5]
